extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, writers, and literary/psychological researchers interested in archetypes and their use in literature, psychology, and marketing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and conceptual criteria for identifying, applying, and interpreting archetypes in literature and related creative work, drawing on Jungian theory, literary criticism, and marketing applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage of archetypes in specific pieces of writing (Function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage of archetypes in specific pieces of writing is a holistic approach, which can help the writing win universal acceptance. This is because readers can relate to and identify with the characters and the situation, both socially and culturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By deploying common archetypes contextually, a writer aims to impart realism to their work. Use archetypes to create situations and characters readers recognize; ensure contextual deployment so archetypal resonance reinforces realism rather than feeling clichéd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story archetypes / Seven basic plots (Christopher Booker)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following basic archetypes underlie all stories: Overcoming the Monster; Rags to Riches; The Quest; Voyage and Return; Comedy; Tragedy; Rebirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These broad plot-structure archetypes can be used as organizing templates for narrative design. Recognize which fundamental plot your story aligns with and how archetypal expectations can be fulfilled or inverted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal literary criticism principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypal literary criticism argues that archetypes determine the form and function of literary works and that a text's meaning is shaped by cultural and psychological myths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify recurring images, symbols, motifs (e.g., quest, heavenly ascent), recognizable character types (trickster, saint, martyr, hero), and symbols (apple, snake) that pre-exist the work and shape readers' interpretation. Use this to analyze how cultural archetypes structure meaning; be aware of unsourced generalizations and cultural specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: archetype as statement/pattern/prototype/recurring motif
rubrics_metrics.description: An archetype can be a statement, pattern of behavior, prototype, 'first' form, or a constantly-recurring symbol or motif in literature, painting, or mythology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or analyzing work, consider whether an element functions as a prototype or recurring motif across contexts. Distinguish archetypal functions from mere cliché by examining recurrence across cultures or deep psychological resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypes as analogies to instincts and drivers of behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypes are very close analogies to instincts, in that, long before any consciousness develops, impersonal and inherited traits present and motivate human behavior. They also continue to influence feelings and behavior after consciousness develops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use archetypes to motivate character behavior from deep, often pre-conscious drives; ensure actions reflect archetypal drives to achieve psychological plausibility. Beware of flattening characters into one-dimensional instincts—combine archetypal motivation with individual detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jungian archetypes and their conceptualization
rubrics_metrics.description: In Jung's psychological framework, archetypes are innate, libidinally collective schemas, universal prototypes for idea-sensory impression images; a group of memories and interpretations associated with an archetype is a complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider archetypes as tendencies to form variable representations rather than fixed mythic images ('the archetype is a tendency to form such representations'). Use Jungian archetypes to inform symbolism and unconscious dynamics in characters and narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Jungian archetypes (primordial images)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four major archetypes from Jung's work include the anima/animus, the self, the shadow, and the persona; Jung also referred to images of the wise old man, the child, the mother, and the maiden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map character roles and internal psychological structures onto these archetypal patterns (e.g., shadow as repressed traits). Employ them to craft inner conflict and thematic resonance; be mindful of cultural variance and not mistaking archetypal representation for literal inheritance of images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neo-Jungian 12 archetypes (Carol Pearson / Margaret Mark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twelve archetypes organized in three overarching categories: Ego types (Innocent, Orphan/Regular person, Hero, Caregiver), Soul types (Explorer, Rebel, Lover, Creator), Self types (Jester, Sage, Magician, Ruler).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 12-archetype schema as a practical toolkit for character design, branding, and narrative roles. Selecting an archetype helps define motivations and tonal choices; consider combining or subverting archetypes for complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded archetype families (Hartwell & Chen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the 12 archetypes can be extended into families of five archetypes (e.g., Innocent Family: Innocent, Child, Dreamer, Idealist, Muse; Citizen Family: Citizen, Advocate, Everyman, Networker, Servant; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use family groupings to nuance character types—pick sibling archetypal facets to diversify a character within a broader archetypal family. This supports creating archetypal variation while maintaining recognizable roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypes reveal shared societal roles and can create stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: The archetypes reveal shared roles universal among societies, such as the role of the mother; these archetypes create a shared imagery defined by many stereotypes that have not separated themselves from traditional, biological, religious, and mythical frameworks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage archetypal roles to tap into shared cultural imagery but guard against perpetuating unexamined stereotypes: contextualize and complicate archetypal roles to avoid reductive portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypes have multiple manifestations and context-dependent functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every archetype has multiple manifestations, with each one featuring different attributes; the function of the archetype must be approached according to context (for example, biological sciences vs. literary usage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt archetypal deployment to genre, culture, and medium; test whether a given manifestation serves the story's ultimate function. Avoid one-size-fits-all application—specify which manifestation is operative in your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of archetypes in marketing (Dichter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying universal themes (archetypes) to products promoted easier discovery and stronger loyalty for brands (Ernest Dichter's marketing application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For brand storytelling or commercial fiction, select archetypal narratives/themes that align with product identity to foster recognition and loyalty. Use ethical caution when manipulating archetypes for commercial persuasion.
